in_lieu.quote: The alternative taxes imposed by §§ 10-35-18, 10-35-19, and 10-35-19.1, are in lieu of all taxes levied by the state, counties, municipalities, school districts, or other political subdivisions of the state on the personal and real property of the company which is used or intended for use as a renewable facility, but are not in lieu of the retail sales and service tax imposed by chapter 10-45, the use tax imposed by chapter 10-46, or any other tax.

rules.quote: Any company owning or holding under lease, or otherwise, real or personal property used, or intended for use, as a wind farm producing power for the first time after June 30, 2007, or a solar facility, shall pay an annual tax equal to three dollars multiplied by the nameplate capacity of the renewable facility.
rules.quote2: "Nameplate capacity," the number of kilowatts a renewable facility can produce, as assigned to the power units in the renewable facility by the manufacturer and determined by the secretary; [...] "Wind farm," all real or personal property used or constructed for the purpose of producing electricity for commercial purposes utilizing the wind as an energy source and with a nameplate capacity of at least five thousand kilowatts.
rules.arithmetic: three dollars a kilowatt is USD 3,000 a MW; a wind farm or solar facility is at least 5,000 kW (5 MW)
rules.not_modeled: The proration of the first year (the tax begins the first calendar year the facility has gross receipts): the tool charges whole operating years.
rules.tip: South Dakota: a wind farm or solar facility of 5 MW or more pays USD 3 per kW of nameplate capacity a year, in lieu of property tax (Codified Laws 10-35-17, -18).

rules.quote: Any company owning or holding under lease, or otherwise, real or personal property used, or intended for use, as a wind farm producing power for the first time after March 31, 2015, shall pay an annual tax of $.00045 per kilowatt hour of electricity produced by the wind farm.
rules.arithmetic: USD 0.00045 per kWh is USD 0.45 per MWh
rules.tip: South Dakota: and USD 0.00045 per kWh produced by wind (USD 0.45 per MWh) (Codified Laws 10-35-19.1).

rules.quote: Any company owning or holding under lease, or otherwise, real or personal property used, or intended for use, as a solar facility, shall pay an annual tax of $.00090 per kilowatt hour of electricity produced by the solar facility.
rules.arithmetic: USD 0.00090 per kWh is USD 0.90 per MWh
rules.tip: South Dakota: and USD 0.0009 per kWh produced by solar (USD 0.90 per MWh) (Codified Laws 10-35-19.1).

rules.quote: (1)(a) The owner of a renewable energy generation facility annually shall pay a nameplate capacity tax equal to the total nameplate capacity of the commissioned renewable energy generation facility multiplied by a tax rate of three thousand five hundred eighteen dollars per megawatt.
rules.exempt_owners: (2) No tax shall be imposed on a renewable energy generation facility or energy storage resource: (a) Owned or operated by the federal government, the State of Nebraska, a public power district, a public power and irrigation district, an individual municipality, a registered group of municipalities, an electric membership association, or a cooperative
rules.not_modeled: Which technologies are a renewable energy generation facility is defined in section 77-6201, not read by this chain: the tool applies the rule to wind and solar and not to geothermal until it is read. Whether the tax replaces the property tax on the equipment is not stated in 77-6203 (not read elsewhere): the tool computes no other property tax in Nebraska. The proration of the first year.
rules.tip: Nebraska: nameplate capacity tax of USD 3,518 per MW a year on renewable generating facilities (Revised Statutes 77-6203).

rules.quote: 1. Wind generators, wind farms, and associated collector systems are subject to taxes consisting of the following two components: a. A tax of two dollars and fifty cents per kilowatt times the rated capacity of the wind generator.
rules.arithmetic: USD 2.50 a kW is USD 2,500 a MW
rules.not_modeled: A company taxed under chapter 57-06 (a centrally assessed utility) is not a company of this chapter unless it elected to be one by 1 October 2013 to 2016 (57-33.2-01(3)); the tool applies the chapter to every owner.
rules.tip: North Dakota: a wind generator pays USD 2.50 per kW of capacity a year, in lieu of property tax except on land (Century Code 57-33.2-04, -05).

rules.quote: b. A tax of one-half of one mill per kilowatt-hour of electricity generated by the wind generator during the taxable period.
rules.arithmetic: one-half of one mill (USD 0.0005) a kWh is USD 0.50 a MWh
rules.tip: North Dakota: and half a mill per kWh produced (USD 0.50 per MWh) (Century Code 57-33.2-04).

rules.quote: 2. Grid-connected generators that are part of a project with generation capacity of one hundred kilowatts or more not produced from coal or wind, or produced from coal and not subject to coal conversion taxes under chapter 57-60, are subject to taxes consisting of the following two components: a. Fifty cents per kilowatt times the rated capacity of the generation unit.
rules.arithmetic: USD 0.50 a kW is USD 500 a MW; a project of 100 kW (0.1 MW) or more
rules.tip: North Dakota: a generator of 100 kW or more from a source other than coal or wind pays 50 cents per kW of capacity a year, in lieu of property tax except on land (Century Code 57-33.2-04, -05).

rules.quote: b. One mill per kilowatt-hour of electricity generated by the production unit during the taxable period.
rules.arithmetic: one mill (USD 0.001) a kWh is USD 1 a MWh
rules.not_modeled: Geothermal holds no capacity factor in the tool, so its production tax is not computed (the capacity tax is).
rules.tip: North Dakota: and one mill per kWh produced (USD 1 per MWh) (Century Code 57-33.2-04).

rules.quote: Any exemption granted under the provisions of this subsection for such property when the applicant, after December 31, 2016, has filed such application or filed such application and received a conditional use permit, shall be in effect for the 10 taxable years immediately following the taxable year in which construction or installation of such property is completed. For purposes of this section, "renewable energy resources or technologies" shall include wind, solar, photovoltaic, biomass, hydropower, geothermal and landfill gas resources or technologies.
rules.not_modeled: The exemption is granted by the Board of Tax Appeals on application; the tool assumes it is granted. After the ten years the property is taxed like other property, and no rule for that is held: the reader's own rate fills those years. Payments in lieu agreed with a county during the exemption (Jayhawk's USD 2,000 per MW, section 9 of the note) are agreements, not the statute.
rules.tip: Kansas: property generating electricity from wind, solar or geothermal is exempt for the 10 taxable years after construction (K.S.A. 79-201, Eleventh); no rule is held after them.

rules.quote: Sec. 1. (1)(a) The governing body of a county and the owner or person in possession or control of a solar project located within the county and outside the boundaries of any incorporated city may enter into an agreement that exempts from property taxes the property constituting the solar project and allows the payment of a fee in lieu of property taxes imposed on the property. (b) An agreement entered into under this section: (A) May not be for a term longer than 20 consecutive years; [...] (2) The fee in lieu of property taxes shall be computed at a rate not less than $5,500, and not more than $7,000, per megawatt of nameplate capacity of the solar project for each property tax year.
rules.quote2: Sec. 3. (1) Section 1, chapter 571, Oregon Laws 2015, is repealed on January 2, 2028. (2) Notwithstanding subsection (1) of this section, property constituting a solar project that is exempt from property taxes under section 1, chapter 571, Oregon Laws 2015, on the date specified in subsection (1) of this section shall continue to be exempt and to pay the fee in lieu of property taxes for the term specified in the agreement
rules.default_why: USD 7,000, the statute's maximum, which was its one fixed rate until the 2021 amendment set the range (a ruling)
rules.not_modeled: The agreement is the county's and the owner's: the tool offers it as a choice, off by default. The repeal of 2 January 2028: a project must be exempt under an agreement by then; the tool does not test the date. After the agreement's years no rule is held (no life total unless the reader types a rate). The land's treatment, which the agreement sets.
rules.tip: Oregon: a county and a solar project outside any city may agree to exempt it for up to 20 years for a fee of USD 5,500 to 7,000 per MW a year (Oregon Laws 2015, chapter 571, in the notes to ORS 307.175).
rules.option_tip: Oregon (2015 c.571, notes to ORS 307.175): a county and a solar project outside any city may agree to exempt it and take a fee in lieu, USD 5,500 to 7,000 per MW of nameplate a year, for up to 20 years; agreements end with projects exempt by 2 January 2028.
rules.rate_tip: Within the statute's USD 5,500 to 7,000 (a rate outside it is held to it). Default 7,000, the statute's maximum and its one fixed rate until the 2021 amendment set the range.

rules.quote: 39-22-103. Imposition. There is levied an excise tax upon the privilege of producing electricity from wind resources in this state. [...] The tax shall be imposed on each megawatt hour of electricity produced from wind resources at the point of interconnection with an electric transmission line. 39-22-104. Taxation rate. The tax rate shall be one dollar ($1.00) on each megawatt hour, or portion thereof, which is produced in this state.
rules.quote2: 39-22-105. (b) Electricity produced from a wind turbine shall not be subject to the tax imposed under this chapter until the date three (3) years after the turbine first produced electricity for sale.
rules.not_modeled: An excise on production, in addition to the property tax on the plant, which no rule here holds: the reader's own property tax rate, if typed, is added to it. MWh at the point of interconnection are taken as the plant's MWh. The three years are counted as the first three operating years.
rules.tip: Wyoming: wind generation excise of USD 1 per MWh, owed from three years after first sale (W.S. 39-22-103 to -105), in addition to the property tax, which is not held.
rules.own_tip: The state's excise on production is held; the property tax on the plant is not: a rate typed here is the reader's own, added to the excise, applied to the capital cost as it falls.

rules.quote: 196.182 Exemption of renewable energy source devices. (1) Eighty percent of the assessed value of a renewable energy source device, as defined in s. 193.624, that is considered tangible personal property is exempt from ad valorem taxation if the renewable energy source device: (a) Is installed on real property on or after January 1, 2018; [...] (4) This section expires December 31, 2037.
rules.quote2: the term "renewable energy source device" means any of the following equipment that collects, transmits, stores, or uses solar energy, wind energy, or energy derived from geothermal deposits or biogas [...]: (a) Solar energy collectors, photovoltaic modules, and inverters. [...] (i) Pipes, ducts, wiring, structural supports, refrigerant handling systems, and other components used as integral parts of such systems [...] (j) Windmills and wind turbines. (k) Wind-driven generators.
rules.not_modeled: No rate is in the statute: the exemption acts on the reader's own rate, applied to the remaining 20 percent of the base through 2037 and to all of it after (the section expires 31 December 2037). The tool applies the 80 percent to the whole capital cost; land and any other real property improvement are not exempt. The fiscally constrained counties' projects filed by 2017 (subsection 2) are not modeled.
rules.tip: Florida: 80 percent of a renewable energy source device's assessed value is exempt, for devices installed from 2018, until the section expires on 31 December 2037 (Statutes 196.182); no rate is in the statute.
rules.own_tip: Florida exempts 80 percent of a renewable energy device's assessed value through 2037 (Statutes 196.182): a rate typed here is the reader's own, applied to the remaining 20 percent of the capital cost until 2037 and to all of it after, as the value falls. Land and other real property are not exempt; the tool applies the 80 percent to the whole capital cost.

rules.quote: A. Through December 31, 2040, the department shall determine the full cash value of taxable renewable energy and storage equipment in the manner prescribed by this section. B. The full cash value of renewable energy and storage equipment is twenty percent of the depreciated cost of the equipment. Depreciated cost shall be determined by deducting depreciation from taxable original cost. Depreciation shall not exceed ninety percent of the adjusted original cost.
rules.quote2: 6. "Taxable original cost" means the original cost reduced by the value of any investment tax credits, production tax credits or cash grants in lieu of investment tax credits applicable to the taxable renewable energy and storage equipment.
rules.not_modeled: No rate is in the section (the assessment ratio and the local rates are elsewhere): it acts on the reader's own rate, applied to 20 percent of the capital cost as it falls, through 2040, and to the whole after. Not modeled: the depreciation cap of 90 percent (the reader's straight line goes to 0), the department's useful lives, and the taxable original cost's reduction by federal tax credits, which the tool does not hold (the base is the capital cost before any credit).
rules.tip: Arizona: renewable energy equipment is valued at 20 percent of its depreciated cost through 2040 (Revised Statutes 42-14155); no rate is in the statute.
rules.own_tip: Arizona values renewable energy equipment at 20 percent of its depreciated cost through 2040 (Revised Statutes 42-14155): a rate typed here is the reader's own, applied to 20 percent of the capital cost until 2040 and to all of it after, as the value falls. The statute's 90 percent cap on depreciation and its deduction of federal tax credits from the cost are not modeled.

rules.quote: The following classes of property are designated special classes under Article V, Sec. 2(2), of the North Carolina Constitution and are excluded from tax: [...] (45) Eighty percent (80%) of the appraised value of a solar energy electric system. For purposes of this subdivision, the term "solar energy electric system" means all equipment used directly and exclusively for the conversion of solar energy to electricity.
rules.not_modeled: No rate is in the section and it has no end date: it acts on the reader's own rate, applied to 20 percent of the capital cost in every year. The tool applies the 80 percent to the whole capital cost; equipment not used directly and exclusively for the conversion, and the land, are taxed in full, which the tool does not separate.
rules.tip: North Carolina: 80 percent of a solar energy electric system's appraised value is excluded from tax (General Statutes 105-275(45)); no rate is in the statute.
rules.own_tip: North Carolina excludes 80 percent of the appraised value of a solar energy electric system from tax (General Statutes 105-275(45)), with no end date: a rate typed here is the reader's own, applied to 20 percent of the capital cost as the value falls. Equipment not used directly for the conversion, and the land, are taxed in full; the tool applies the 80 percent to the whole capital cost.

rules.tip: Tennessee: power companies, solar and wind included, are assessed by the Comptroller as public utilities at 55 percent; solar property is valued initially at no more than 12.5 percent of its installed cost with a green energy certification or a filing under 67-5-1303 (T.C.A. 67-5-601, Schedule EL-SOL; Comptroller's glossary). The 12.5 percent is held in every year: an upper bound after the first.
rules.quote: Solar sourced property values should not initially exceed twelve and one half percent (12.5%) of total installed cost if a green energy production facility certification issued by the department of environment and conservation is on file, or filing of a schedule or statement pursuant to § 67-5-1303 [...] Public utility property 55%

rules.tip: Tennessee: power companies are assessed by the Comptroller as public utilities, at 55 percent of value (the Comptroller's FAQ and assessment glossary, read 13 November 2026). The value is held at the capital cost, without depreciation (no schedule read): an upper bound.
rules.quote: Power companies, including hydroelectric, steam, and atomic power [...] green sources that produce electricity, such as geothermal, hydrogen, solar and wind companies [...] 55 percent of its value for public utility property

rules.tip: New Mexico: taxable value is one third of full value (NMSA 7-37-3), electric plant valued by the Department at cost less straight-line depreciation, not below 20 percent of cost (7-36-29, as 2016 SB 47 shows it); industrial revenue bonds may exempt a plant by local approval (not modeled). The value is held at the capital cost, without depreciation (no schedule read): an upper bound.
rules.quote: The tax ratio is thirty-three and one-third percent (33-1/3%).

rules.tip: South Carolina: property of manufacturers and utilities is assessed at 10.5 percent of fair market value (Code 12-43-220(a)(1)); a fee in lieu agreed with the county (chapter 44) is not modeled. The value is held at the capital cost, without depreciation (no schedule read): an upper bound.
rules.quote: must be taxed on an assessment equal to ten and one-half percent of the fair market value of the property

rules.tip: South Carolina: and an excise of half a mill per kWh of power sold for resale in the state (USD 0.50 per MWh) (Code 12-23-10).
rules.quote: is subject to the payment of an excise, license, or privilege tax of five-tenths of one mill [...] upon each kilowatt hour of electric power sold for resale within the State

rules.tip: Texas: appraisal districts value property at market value as of 1 January (Tax Code 23.01, as the Comptroller states it); local abatements (chapter 312) and school value limitations (JETI) are negotiated and not modeled. The value is held at the capital cost, without depreciation (no schedule read): an upper bound.
rules.quote: Tax Code Section 23.01 requires appraisal districts to appraise taxable property at market value as of Jan. 1.
rules.levy_words: Texas: no statewide figure; the Comptroller publishes rates by taxing unit. The sum of your county's, school district's and other units' rates per 1,000 of value.

rules.tip: Ohio: an energy company's production equipment first taxed for tax year 2027 is assessed at 7 percent of true value (R.C. 5727.111, as the Legislative Service Commission's analysis of H.B. 96 states it); payments in lieu under R.C. 5727.75 continue for existing projects only. The value falls by the Department of Taxation's Class C-30 composite allowances, 98.3 percent good at age 1 to 15 percent at 30 (2025 instructions).
rules.quote: the tangible personal property (TPP) assessment rate of a rural electric company or energy company's production or energy conversion equipment that is first subject to taxation for tax year 2027, or that is repowered or converted production equipment, is 7%.
rules.quote2: The minimum percent good for taxable property in any class is 15%. [...] All other production plant equipment uses Class C-30. [...] Age C-5 C-7.5 C-10 C-15 C-20 C-25 C-30 [...] 1 90.0 93.3 95.0 96.7 97.5 98.0 98.3

rules.tip: New York: a solar or wind system's added value is exempt from real property tax for 15 years where built before 1 January 2030, unless the municipality opts out or requires a payment in lieu of up to 15 years, not above the tax otherwise due (RPTL 487); after it the state's appraisal model applies (RPTL 575-b).
rules.own_tip: New York: a solar or wind system's added value is exempt for 15 years where built before 1 January 2030, unless the town has opted out or requires a payment in lieu, which may not exceed the tax otherwise due (RPTL 487): a rate typed here is the reader's own, charged after the 15 years (and from the start where the town has opted out, by setting the start after 2029).
rules.quote: shall be exempt from taxation to the extent of any increase in the value thereof [...] for a period of fifteen years [...] constructed subsequent to January first, nineteen hundred ninety-one and prior to January first, two thousand thirty [...] Any payment in lieu of a tax agreement shall not operate for a period of more than fifteen years
rules.not_modeled: Read by the subagent from nysenate.gov; this chain's own read was refused (HTTP 403) and not retried. The local opt-out and payments in lieu are local; the appraisal model after the 15 years (a discounted cash flow) is not modeled: the reader's own rate stands for it.

rules.tip: New York: power generating apparatus is real property taxed at local rates (RPTL 102(12)(f)); no statewide rate read: no rule held.

Pennsylvania: wind turbines, towers and their foundations are not real property and are not assessed; the land is valued by capitalizing its lease income (53 Pa.C.S. 8811(b)(5), 8842(b)(2)): USD 0 on the equipment, the land not modeled.
rules.quote: No wind turbine generators or related wind energy appliances and equipment, including towers and tower foundations, shall be considered or included as part of the real property in determining the fair market value and assessment of real property used for the purpose of wind energy generation.

rules.tip: Pennsylvania: counties assess real property at a ratio up to 100 percent (53 Pa.C.S. 8842); machinery in an industrial establishment is not real estate (8811(b)(1)); whether that reaches a solar or gas plant was not read: no rule held.

District of Columbia: a system using exclusively solar energy is exempt from personal property tax (FP-31 instructions, 2026; D.C. Code 47-1508(a)); its real property is taxed at USD 1.65 to 1.89 per 100.
rules.own_tip: District of Columbia: a solar system is exempt from personal property tax (FP-31 instructions, 2026): the tool's base, the capital cost, is held exempt; a rate typed here does not apply to it.
rules.quote: You are a system using exclusively solar energy as defined in DC Official Code § 34-1431(14).

rules.tip: District of Columbia: business personal property is taxed on its straight-line remaining cost, not below 25 percent of cost, above an exclusion of USD 225,000 (FP-31 instructions, 2026); the rate is not stated and the D.C. Code refuses automated reads: no rule held.

Alabama: utility property is Class I, assessed at 30 percent, other property Class II at 20 percent (Constitution, as the Department of Revenue's assessment page states it, read 13 November 2026); a merchant plant's class is not stated and abatements (Code 40-9B) are discretionary: no rule held.

Alaska: no state property tax on a generating plant; boroughs and cities levy up to 30 mills (AS 29.45.090, as Legislative Research Report 21.028 states it); the statutes and the Department of Revenue refuse automated reads: no rule held.
Arkansas: the code is published through LexisNexis and the Department of Finance's manuals could not be read (13 November 2026): no rule held.

Colorado: renewable facilities are valued by an income approach with a tax factor for 30 years (SB21-020, C.R.S. 39-4-102) and assessed at 25 to 27 percent (HB24B-1001); the Division of Property Taxation refuses automated reads: no rule held.

Connecticut: a Class I renewable source is exempt only up to its site's load; towns may abate up to 100 percent under a state-directed purchase contract (CGS 12-81(57), Office of Legislative Research Report 2023-R-0214); the statute site could not be read: no rule held.
Delaware: counties assess property at fair market value, reassessed at least every 5 years (9 Del. C. 8306); no rule for generating plants and no statewide rate read: no rule held.

Hawaii: a public utility pays the public service company tax on gross income in place of most taxes (HRS 239-2, 239-5); whether an independent producer is one (HRS 269-1) could not be read, and the tool holds no sale price: no rule held.

Idaho: wind and geothermal producers pay 3 percent and solar producers 3.5 percent of gross energy earnings, in place of property tax (Code 63-3502B, 63-602JJ); the tool holds no sale price: no rule held (ruling 16).
Indiana: the Code site serves no statute text to automated reads and the Department of Local Government Finance's guidance could not be read (13 November 2026): no rule held.

Louisiana: public service property is assessed at 25 percent and other property at 15 percent of fair market value (Constitution article VII, section 18); whether a merchant plant is public service property is not stated, and the industrial tax exemption is discretionary: no rule held.

Massachusetts: plants are taxed locally at fair cash value (G.L. c. 59, s. 38); utility-scale solar and wind are exempt for 20 years only under a negotiated payment in lieu (c. 59, s. 5, cl. 45): no rule held.
Maine: plants selling most of their output are outside the business equipment exemption (36 M.R.S. 691) and pay local tax at just value (701-A); no statewide rate could be read: no rule held.
Missouri: the State Tax Commission assesses utilities' distributable property (RSMo 138.420 and chapters 151 to 155, as its 2024 report states); the statutes' text could not be read: no rule held.

Mississippi: public utility property is Class IV, assessed at 30 percent, other property at 15 percent (Constitution article 4, section 112, as the Department of Revenue states it); a merchant plant's class is not stated and local exemptions of up to 10 years (Code 27-31-101) are discretionary: no rule held.

New Hampshire: generating property of a company that neither transmits nor distributes leaves the state utility property tax on 1 July 2027 (RSA 83-F:1, as amended 2025); towns tax it at full and true value (RSA 75:1) or agree a voluntary payment in lieu (72:74): no rule held.

New Jersey: machinery and equipment used in business is not real property and is not taxed (N.J.S.A. 54:4-1, as the Handbook for New Jersey Assessors states it); land and structures are taxed locally; the 1997 restructuring law was not read: no rule held.
Oklahoma: both statute sites refuse automated reads (their robots files) and the Tax Commission's manuals could not be read (13 November 2026): no rule held.
Utah: the State Tax Commission centrally assesses utility property (Code 59-2-201); the Code pages serve no text to automated reads: no rule held.
